procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Bombay High Court dated September 16, 1966 in Criminal Appeal No. 1349 of 1965, which approved the Magistrate's decision to examine the Customs Officer (Dutta) under s. 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant appealed to the Bombay High Court against his conviction by the trial court under Sections 135(a) and 135(b) of the Customs Act, 1962. The High Court dismissed the appeal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's approval of the Magistrate's decision to examine the Customs Officer (Dutta) under s. 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The question before the Supreme Court was whether the evidence of the officer was improperly received by the Magistrate and whether if excluded the conviction of the appellant could be supported.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court's power under Section 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to summon a witness at any stage is absolute and can be exercised even after the prosecution has closed its case, if the court deems it necessary for a just decision.

facts: After the defence case was closed, the prosecution sought to call an additional witness.
The trial magistrate allowed the witness to be called, stating that the evidence was 'necessary for the just decision of the case'.
The magistrate also permitted the accused to be further examined and to lead additional evidence in response.
The appellant challenged this decision, arguing that the court's power under Section 540 should not be used to allow the prosecution to fill a gap in its case after the defence is over.
law: Section 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure grants a court the power to summon a witness at any stage of a trial.
The section is divided into two parts: a discretionary first part (using the word 'may') and a mandatory second part (using the word 'shall').
The first part gives the court discretion to summon, examine, or recall any witness.
The second part makes it obligatory for the court to take such action if the evidence appears 'essential to the just decision of the case'.
The text emphasizes that the repeated use of the word 'any' indicates the power is intended to be wide and is not limited by the stage the trial has reached.
This power can be exercised to benefit either the prosecution or the accused, as long as it serves the purpose of a just decision.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the trial judge had exercised his power under the second, mandatory part of Section 540, as he explicitly found the evidence to be 'essential to the just decision of the case'.
The Court rejected the argument that the procedural rules of a trial (like the closing of the defence case) could limit the absolute power conferred by Section 540.

It held that the key criterion for exercising power under the second part is not whether the defence was surprised, but whether the court genuinely believes the new evidence is necessary for a just decision.

The Court affirmed that as long as the trial court is bona fide of the opinion that the evidence is essential for a just decision, there is no limitation on its power to summon a witness at any stage.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that the court's power under Section 540 is wide and can be exercised at any stage of the trial, even after the defence has closed its case. It held that the section's second part is mandatory, compelling a court to summon a witness if it deems their evidence essential for a just decision, irrespective of the trial's stage.

issue.issue_text: Whether the evidence of the seizing officer was improperly received by the Magistrate when the officer was called as a court witness after the prosecution had concluded its case.

facts: The appellant's shop was searched, and numerous watches and clocks were seized under the Customs Act, 1962.
The appellant was prosecuted for possessing smuggled goods but did not present any evidence in his defense.

After the prosecution concluded its case, the appellant filed a written statement arguing that the prosecution had failed to prove a necessary element: that the goods were seized under the "reasonable belief" that they were smuggled. This proof was required under s. 123 of the Act to shift the burden of proof to the accused.
In response, the prosecution requested that the seizing officer (Dutta) be examined as a court witness.
Over the appellant's objection, the Magistrate granted the request under s. 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, stating the officer's evidence was "necessary for the just decision of the case."
The officer then testified that he had seized the goods with the reasonable belief that they were smuggled.
The appellant was given the opportunity to cross-examine the officer and present further defense evidence but declined to do so.
law: The case centered on Section 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
This section grants a court the power to summon and examine any person as a witness at any stage of a trial.
The section has two parts: a discretionary power to call a witness, and a mandatory duty to do so if that witness's evidence "appears to it essential to the just decision of the case."
The Court noted that this power is conferred in absolute terms and is not limited by the stage the trial has reached.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the Magistrate had exercised his power under the second, mandatory part of s. 540, concluding that the officer's evidence was essential for a just decision.

The Court reasoned that the central issue was whether the goods were smuggled. The circumstances of the seizure already strongly suggested that the seizing officer must have held a belief that they were. Therefore, hearing the officer's testimony on this point was crucial for the court to make a fair and just ruling.

The Court rejected the appellant's argument that the prosecution was simply trying to "fill a gap" in its case. It viewed the situation as the court itself needing to hear the evidence to properly decide the case, rather than the prosecution fixing an error.
The Court held that the test under s. 540 is not whether the new evidence arises unexpectedly, but whether the court genuinely believes it is needed for a just decision.

Furthermore, the Court found no injustice was done to the appellant, as he was given a full opportunity to cross-examine the new witness and present his own evidence in rebuttal, which he chose not to do.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the Magistrate had properly exercised his power under s. 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The evidence of the seizing officer was deemed essential for a just decision of the case, and therefore, it was not improperly received, even though it was introduced after the prosecution had closed its case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the court's power under Section 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to summon a witness at any stage is absolute and can be exercised even after the prosecution has closed its case, if the court deems it necessary for a just decision.
appellant_arguments: The power under Section 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, while wide, is not absolute and must not be exercised to the disadvantage of the accused.
This power should not be used after the accused's defence is over, particularly to fill a crucial gap in the prosecution's case that the defence has already pointed out.
Case law establishes that exercising this power to the detriment of the accused after the defence has been disclosed is improper.
respondent_arguments: The power under Section 540 is intentionally wide to allow the court to summon any witness at any stage if their evidence is essential for a just decision.
The court has a duty to ascertain the truth, and this power is a tool to achieve that, which can be exercised even after the prosecution has closed its case.
Case law supports a liberal interpretation of the court's powers under this section to ensure justice is done.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the evidence of the seizing officer was improperly received by the Magistrate when the officer was called as a court witness after the prosecution had concluded its case.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution failed to establish a key element of its case: that the goods were seized under the 'reasonable belief' that they were smuggled, which is required under s. 123 of the Customs Act to shift the burden of proof.
Calling the seizing officer to testify about his belief only after the appellant pointed out this omission in his written statement was an attempt to fill a fatal gap in the prosecution's case.
Allowing this evidence at such a late stage was prejudicial to the accused and an unfair use of the court's power.
respondent_arguments: The examination of the seizing officer was not to fill a gap, but was essential for the 'just decision of the case' to formally place the officer's belief on record.
The circumstances of the seizure already on record strongly implied that the officer had a reasonable belief the goods were smuggled; calling him as a witness was to confirm this under oath.
The appellant was not prejudiced, as he was re-examined after the new evidence was introduced and was given an opportunity to lead his own defence evidence, which he declined.

cases.principle: Cited as the foundational decision establishing the court's power to call evidence in aid of a just decision, which cannot be regarded as exceeding jurisdiction.
Cited as a case that applied the principle from Reg. v. Frost regarding the court's power to call evidence at any stage to ensure a just decision.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Statutory law confers an absolute power, duty, and obligation on a court to be exercised at any stage of a trial to summon, examine, or recall a witness, provided the court believes it is necessary for a just decision of the case. The inquiry is not whether the accused has introduced something sudden or unexpected, but whether the court itself needs the new evidence for a just decision.
obiter: The power under the Indian Code is not limited to cases involving something arising ex-improviso which no human ingenuity could foresee.
If the court has acted without the requirements of a just decision, the action is open to criticism.
It is not right to embark on judicial legislation by adding conditions, such as the ex-improviso rule, that are not present in the Code.
Even in England, courts have allowed fresh evidence for a just decision, and an appellate court would not interfere with a judge's discretion to recall a witness unless it caused an injustice.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The power conferred on a court under Section 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is absolute and is not limited by the stage of the trial. It is both a power and a duty for the court to summon or recall a witness if it is bona fide of the opinion that such evidence is essential for the just decision of the case. The inquiry is not whether the defence has raised an unexpected point, but whether the court itself needs the evidence to reach a just conclusion.
legal_tests_applied: The test for exercising power under the second part of Section 540 is not whether something has arisen 'ex-improviso' which could not be foreseen, but whether the court is right in thinking that the new evidence is needed by it for a just decision of the case.
If the court's action is supportable as being in aid of a just decision, the action cannot be regarded as exceeding its jurisdiction.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument to limit the court's power to situations arising 'ex-improviso' (unexpectedly) was rejected, as the court found that the Indian Code does not contain this condition and it would be improper judicial legislation to add it.

The court determined that this was not a case of the prosecution trying to fill a gap in its case, but rather the court itself acting to ensure a just decision by having the seizing officer's belief placed on the record under oath.

The court found that the action was not an unfair advantage to the prosecution, as the circumstances already on record strongly implied the officer's belief; calling the witness merely formalized this essential fact for the court's consideration.
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed that Indian statutory law confers a power in absolute terms to be exercised at any stage of the trial, provided the just decision of the case demands it.
The trial judge was found to have correctly exercised his power under the second part of Section 540, as the evidence of the seizing officer was deemed essential to the just decision of the case.

The court concluded that a just decision required finding whether the goods were smuggled, and for that, the nature of the belief underlying the seizure needed to be before the court on oath, which justified calling the officer as a court witness.
policy_considerations: The court has a duty and obligation to act in aid of justice, and the power to summon witnesses at any stage is a tool to fulfill that obligation.

It is not right for the judiciary to embark on judicial legislation by reading limitations into the Code, such as the 'ex-improviso' rule from English law, where the statutory language is wide and unconditional.

The court's action was consistent with the policy of the Customs Act, 1962, which requires an accused to prove innocent possession once the prosecution establishes a reasonable belief that the goods were smuggled.
